headline: Medium prompt-injection, leakage, and capability-conflict risks arise from shared filesystem and broad shell/network defaults; no critical compliance issue is evidenced.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGen can read and write working directories and uses stdin/stdout plus tool calls; Plandex also reads/writes the project directory and plan-local sandbox. That creates a plausible file-based bridge where one agent can ingest the other's outputs as trusted content. This is not merely manual copy-paste, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same directory or exchanged files are auto-read, prompt injection becomes reachable.
IF either agent treats file contents as instructions without provenance checks, attacker-controlled text can steer tool use.
mitigations: Use separate directories for each agent.
Disable auto-ingest of newly written files.
Add a human review step before one agent consumes the other's output.
Prefix exchanged files with explicit provenance metadata.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization or instruction/data separation in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch filesystem data and both have broad network egress to model providers or cloud services. AutoGen handles application data and model provider API keys; Plandex touches source code and can call Plandex Cloud or a self-hosted server. If sensitive files are shared, either agent can transmit them outward in default workflows.
conditions: IF sensitive source or application data is placed in the shared workspace, both agents can read it.
IF either agent is configured with external model providers or cloud backends, file contents may leave the local environment.
mitigations: Keep secrets and regulated data out of the shared workspace.
Use local-only model endpoints for both agents.
Restrict network egress at the host or container level.
Mount read-only copies of inputs where possible.
requires-engineering: add DLP or redaction before any outbound API call.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, subprocess spawning, and broad network egress. Plandex additionally can modify git state, while AutoGen can install packages. In a shared project tree, concurrent writes and git mutations can race or overwrite each other, making the default interaction dangerous.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or working directory, write conflicts are reachable.
IF Plandex auto-applies changes while AutoGen is also editing files, git and filesystem state can diverge.
mitigations: Assign disjoint working directories.
Disable auto-apply in Plandex.
Serialize write phases with a lock file or scheduler.
Pause package installation during shared runs.
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination around git and filesystem writes.

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGen produces tool calls and code-execution outputs that Plandex can plausibly consume as plan inputs, and Plandex is designed for review-then-apply workflows. That makes unverified downstream action possible if Plandex treats AutoGen output as authoritative. The pair is not proven to verify each other, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF AutoGen output is piped into Plandex without a verification step, errors can cascade into applied changes.
IF Plandex auto-apply is enabled, unverified suggestions can become filesystem mutations.
mitigations: Require explicit verification before apply.
Keep AutoGen and Plandex outputs in separate review queues.
Disable auto-apply.
Add a checksum or diff review gate between agents.
requires-engineering: implement structured provenance and validation for inter-agent handoffs.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and docs-only, with no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch stated. The only concrete compliance-relevant fact is that both handle model provider API keys and may send data to configured providers, but the pairwise residency breach is not evidenced. One-agent citations suffice because no cross-agent compliance mismatch is documented.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed to a noncompliant external provider, compliance risk increases.
IF the operator configures different retention policies for the two agents on the same data class, policy mismatch becomes material.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in prompts and files.
Use providers with matching compliance attestations.
Align retention settings across both tools.
Document data flows before deployment.
requires-engineering: perform a formal residency and DPA review.
